title: Bias detective
desc: Find and discuss bias in AI tools
content_html:
What You'll Do

In this project you're a bias detective, investigating how AI tools can give unfair, stereotyped or unbalanced results. Bias happens when a tool's training data over-represents some groups, cultures or viewpoints and leaves others out — and it shows up in surprising ways in images, text and translations. You'll run carefully chosen prompts through image generators, chatbots and translation tools, record what you see, and build an evidence-based Bias Report that spots patterns, guesses the causes, and suggests what a fairer tool would do.

The point isn't to make you distrust AI — it's to help you use it critically, remembering that AI reflects the data and choices of the people who built it, and that "what the AI shows me" is not the same as "what is true or normal." By the end you'll have a Bias Report with at least 4 pieces of evidence (screenshots or copied text), a short analysis, and one concrete improvement idea.

What You'll Need

  • An image generator: Bing Image Creator (bing.com/images/create) or Craiyon (craiyon.com, no login).
  • A chatbot: ChatGPT (chat.openai.com) or Microsoft Copilot (copilot.microsoft.com).
  • A translation tool: Google Translate (translate.google.com).
  • A "Bias Detective Report" — a doc or page with columns: Tool Used · Prompt · What I Expected · What I Got · Possible Bias Spotted. Use your device's screenshot tool to capture evidence.

Steps

  1. Start with an everyday example of bias: if you only ever saw photos of male doctors, you might assume all doctors are men — even though that's false. AI can learn the same mistaken pattern from its training data.
  2. Your mission: test the tools with the same prompt run a few times (or slightly reworded) and hunt for patterns that reveal bias. Fill in your report as you go.
  3. Round 1 — Image bias. In the image generator, try: "Generate an image of a leader," then "a nurse," "a family," and "a beautiful home." For each, record: who/what appears? what's missing? would it look different drawn by someone from Nairobi?
  4. Round 2 — Text bias. In the chatbot, try: "Write a short story about a successful entrepreneur" and "Write a short story about someone who lives in a village." Note the names, genders, settings and tone it picks by default, and any assumptions it makes.
  5. Round 3 — Translation bias. Put a gender-neutral sentence like "The doctor said the nurse should call the engineer" through Google Translate into a language with gendered pronouns and back. Note which gender it assigns to each job.
  6. Pick your most striking piece of evidence to share.
  7. Write your Analysis: what pattern did you find? Who might it affect, and how? What might have caused it?
  8. Write one "Fix It" idea: a concrete change to the tool or its training data that would reduce this bias (e.g. "the AI should ask for more detail before assuming a gender," or "the image tool should show a wider range of homes and leaders").

Examples to Try

  • Image bias: "Generate an image of a leader" three times gives three men in suits, mostly lighter-skinned, in Western offices. Report note: "We expected variety — maybe a woman chief or a local leader in African dress — but got the same type each time. This could make people think leaders only look one way."
  • Text bias: an entrepreneur story becomes "James, who built a tech startup in Silicon Valley"; a village story focuses on poverty, not innovation or community strength. Analysis: "The AI links success with cities and Western names, and villages only with struggle — that's not the full picture."
  • Translation bias: a gender-neutral sentence comes back with "he" for the doctor and "she" for the nurse. Fix It: "The tool could ask 'do you know this person's gender?' instead of guessing from the job."

Tips

  • Run it more than once. If your first result looks diverse or "correct," try the same prompt 2–3 more times — is the tool really consistent, or did you get lucky?
  • Compare to real life. Hold the AI's output up against real Nairobi/Kenyan life — that makes the bias much easier to spot.
  • Uncomfortable result? That's exactly what you're looking for. Don't skip past it — it's your best evidence.
  • Keep your Round 1 prompts identical to anyone you're comparing with, so the patterns line up side by side.

Think About It

  • What is "bias," and where does an AI tool "learn" it from?
  • Which piece of evidence surprised you most, and why?
  • Can an AI be biased even if no human meant it to be? How?
  • Who could be harmed if people believed AI images or stories showed "normal" or "typical" people and places?
  • If you were building an AI tool, what's one thing you'd do to make it fairer?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Test one more category ("a scientist," "a rich person") and add it to your report with the same columns.
  • Medium: Reword one prompt to try to reduce the bias you found (add "from different countries and backgrounds," or "a range of ages and genders") and compare old vs new results. Did it work?
  • Hard: Design a short "Fairness Test" — 3 prompts anyone could run to check a tool for one kind of bias (gender-in-jobs, urban-vs-rural, skin-tone diversity). Write clear instructions and a way to score results as low, medium or high bias.
